segments: 1721, the smallox epidemic ravaged the
city of Boston, infecting over half of
its population. Over 800 people died in
Boston alone. But it was the
contributions of an enslaved man named
Onimus who would stop the disease from
wiping out Boston and the rest of the
colonies. Onimus was an African man born
in present-day Ghana who was sold into
slavery to the Boston Puritan Minister
Cotton Mather. The procedure Onimus
described was called varilation which
was a precursor to today's vaccinations.
Onimus brought the method from Africa
who exercised the practice of varilation
for hundreds of years. This involved
rubbing pus from an infected person with
smallpox into an open wound on the arm
of an uninfected individual. Many
critics dismissed the idea simply
because it was introduced by an enslaved
African. But Minister Mather and a local
doctor were desperate to stop the deaths
and decided to move forward with the
inoculations. Onimus' inoculation helped
eradicate smallpox in Boston and saved
thousands of lives in early America.
